description:
We’re a bunch of STEM and tech enthusiasts who love turning crazy ideas into actual projects! This time, we’re taking our creativity to space by building software to help monitor astronauts and keep them safe.

We’re looking for programmers, AI enthusiasts, data analysts and UI/UX designers who enjoy problem-solving, teamwork, and a little bit of chaos.

You don’t have to be an expert; just bring your curiosity, ideas, and willingness to experiment! Ctrl+Z = Big Bang — Houston, we have a team!
summary:
CrewCheck is an app that monitors astronauts’ health during space missions. It monitors their health by combining data from wearables like heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, sleep and activity with self-reported inputs such like fatigue, mood and daily actions.
Our application creates a health baseline for each astronaut. It then tracks how health trends change over time by comparing readings to that individual baseline and sending alerts when something unusual shows up. It also has recovery tracking so that users can see how their health is responding after activity.
The prototype implemented with HTML, CSS and JavaScript to demonstrate the monitoring process with simulated sensor data.
CrewCheck matters because space travel has challenges such as microgravity, radiation, isolation, and disrupted circadian rhythms and much more. These factors severely impact physical and mental well-being of astronauts over time. When missions are far from Earth, communication delays and limited medical intervention make quick decision-making the key. 
CrewCheck enables crew members to spot physiological changes sooner, understand underlying trends, and take proactive health measures. It doesn’t replace medical professionals; it gives them timely useful information.
details:
CrewCheck: Personalized Astronaut Health Monitoring and Mission Adaptation System application

What exactly does our application do?

CrewCheck is a custom health-monitoring and decision support application that helps astronauts monitor their physical and psychological well-being during long-duration space missions. It combines physiological measurements and astronaut reported information to provide a better picture of how a person’s health changes throughout a mission.

The system tracks a number of parameters such as heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, sleep duration, and activity levels. It also captures manual check-ins about fatigue, mood, symptoms, and performed activities. By combining these measurements, CrewCheck combines these measurements to allow astronauts to recognize unusual changes, monitor trends, and get to know their responses to different activities.

How does our application work?

CrewCheck follows a continuous monitoring workflow demonstrated through simulated data in its current prototype.

First, an astronaut has a health profile and baseline for the individual. The application then rgets simulated wearable readings and combines them with manually entered check-ins. JavaScript processes these inputs then compares the readings with the astronaut's personal baseline.

The application shows physiological trends via interactive charts and can generate rule-based alerts when measurements go outside configured thresholds. It can also show recovery monitoring, so you can see the effect of activity on your physiology. Pre-defined recommendations provide guidance if unusual patterns are detected.

Rather than diagnosing medical conditions, CrewCheck highlights changes that may require further attention or medical assessment.

What benefits does our application have?

The long-term presence of astronauts in space poses five major health risks identified by NASA: space radiation, altered gravity, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, and hostile or closed environments. These conditions can affect cardiovascular function, sleep, physical performance and psychological well-being.

CrewCheck fulfills the need for accessibility and personalization in health tracking by:

  • Tracking personal health trends instead of using general thresholds.
  • Including both physical measurements and self-reporting of personal well-being.
  • Making unusual changes easier to spot through visualizations and alerts.
  • providing assistance by knowing how activities and recovery affect personal health
  • Presenting health data in an organized format that can support quick decision-making.

This becomes especially pertinent in the context of deep space explorations in the future, considering the delays in communication and lack of immediate medical help available there.

 What do we hope to achieve?

Our goal is to develop a reliable, personalized health-monitoring framework for astronauts understand how their bodies respond and adapt to the conditions of spaceflight. Our intent is to showcase how integrating physiology, individualized baselines, activity logs, and self-assessments of wellness may enhance health-monitoring efforts.

In future development, CrewCheck could have more advanced recovery analysis, and validated anomaly-detection methods. Ultimately, we aim to contribute to safer and more informed human exploration beyond low Earth orbit.

 What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

The current prototype was made using:

  • HTML5: It builds up the UI and dashboard of the application.
  • CSS3: It supplies the graphic design, layout, and styling of the application.
  • Vanilla JavaScript: Manages the application’s logic, simulated data, user interaction, baseline calculation, and alert generation.
  • HTML Canvas and JavaScript: Displays physiological trends in the form of custom-made graphs.

The prototype utilizes simulated data of the sensors and locally-stored demo data. The prototype is not connected to physical wearable devices and any backend database at the moment. No special hardware was needed for the software prototype.

 

For real-world implementation, CrewCheck would require a combination of wearable biosensors, data-processing devices, and secure onboard storage infrastructure.

 

1. Physiological wearables

The astronauts could wear a smart bio-shirt or a special vest with numerous physiological sensors such as:

PPG sensor (photoplethysmography): It uses light to calculate the heart rate and, in case it is possible due to the equipment used, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2).

ECG electrodes (electrocardiogram): They record the electrical activity of the heart and provide better control of the heart rate and rhythms.

Pulse oximeter: In most cases, it is put on one of the astronaut's fingers; however, it is possible to use it while wearing any special suit.

Temperature sensors: Sensors that can either track skin temperature or monitor the temperature of the core of the body non-invasively.

Accelerometer and gyroscope (three-axis): Sensors that can detect movements, orientation, and physical activities.

Breathing sensors: Special sensors that can calculate the breathing rate and breathing rhythms.

 

2. Additional monitoring sensors

Actigraphy wristband: Detects movements and light exposure in order to estimate sleeping time and circadian rhythms.

 

Blood pressure monitor: Performs regular blood pressure measurement, which will provide cardiovascular monitoring information.

 

Personal radiation dosimeter: Measures the amount of radiation exposure that the astronaut is experiencing; thus, this is one more piece of information about their health status related to the mission, which may be used in the future.

 

3. Data collection and processing hardware

 

The CrewCheck app would run on a tablet computer or other onboard computer, receiving sensor data, processing the results, showing trends in astronauts' health, and allowing them to complete manual wellbeing check-ins.

 

Wearable devices can send data via Bluetooth Low Energy or any other wireless communication protocol. The onboard computer or storage device will keep historical data and will exchange it with medical specialists as long as the connection is available.
